requirements: The core contributions of the paper 'Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve' have been reproduced, including chunked-prefills, stall-free batching, and their capacity/latency improvements over vLLM and Orca across Mistral-7B, Yi-34B, LLaMA2-70B, and Falcon-180B.

sub_tasks.requirements: Sarathi-Serve is buildable and runnable on the paper's hardware configurations (A100 single-node, A100 multi-node cross-network, A40 8-GPU) with CUDA 12.1, NCCL for TP/PP communication, and FlashAttention v2 kernels.
CUDA toolchain and PyTorch environment match the paper's build requirements (CUDA 12.1) and provide a reproducible install path.

Code has been implemented that pins CUDA 12.1 (or a compatible CUDA 12.x runtime) as the target toolchain, either via a Dockerfile, conda env file, or environment setup script that installs matching cudatoolkit / nvcc versions.
Code has been implemented that installs a PyTorch version whose CUDA build is compatible with CUDA 12.1 and that torch.cuda.is_available() returns True after setup on an A100 or A40 host.
A reproduce.sh (or equivalent top-level script) exists that, from a clean checkout, builds the Sarathi-Serve package (including any custom /csrc CUDA kernels) and exits with code 0.
FlashAttention v2 paged-attention kernel backend is wired into the Sarathi-Serve execution path for chunked prefill and decode.
Code has been implemented that imports/links FlashAttention v2 (as stated in §4.4) and exposes a paged chunked-prefill attention kernel selectable as the default backend.

The FlashAttention v2 backend, when invoked on a hybrid batch containing both a decode row and a partial-prefill chunk that references KV-cache from prior chunks of the same prompt, produces numerically correct outputs (within fp16 tolerance vs a reference dense attention on the same inputs).
NCCL-based collective and point-to-point communication is set up for both tensor-parallel and pipeline-parallel deployments.
Code has been implemented that initializes an NCCL process group for TP all-reduce operations and a separate NCCL communicator (or reused group) for PP point-to-point send/recv, as specified in §4.4.
A smoke test exists that runs a 2-GPU TP all-reduce and a 2-stage PP send/recv over NCCL and verifies tensors round-trip correctly, confirming NCCL is functional on the target host.
Hardware-configuration profiles for the four paper deployments are defined and selectable at launch (Table 1).

A configuration/launcher exists for Mistral-7B on 1 A100 (80GB), for Yi-34B on 2 A100s with TP=2, for LLaMA2-70B on 8 A40s with TP=4 PP=2, and for Falcon-180B on 2 nodes of 4 A100s each with TP=4 PP=2, matching Table 1 exactly.

Code has been implemented that, given a hardware profile, verifies at startup the visible GPU count, per-GPU HBM (80GB for A100, 48GB for A40), and CUDA compute capability match the requested configuration and aborts with a clear error otherwise.

Cross-node launching for the Falcon-180B TP4-PP2 deployment across 2 Azure NC96ads v4 nodes is supported via a multi-node launcher (e.g., torchrun with rendezvous or an equivalent), and PP-stage placement uses intra-node NVLink for TP and the 100 Gbps Ethernet link for cross-node PP.
Runtime sanity of end-to-end serving is demonstrable on the target hardware before any experiment is measured.

Code has been implemented that boots the Sarathi-Serve server with a small model (e.g., Mistral-7B on 1 A100), sends a single prompt, and returns a non-empty generated completion, confirming environment + kernels + NCCL are all functional.

For the Falcon-180B TP4-PP2 configuration on 2 A100 nodes over 100 Gbps Ethernet, decode-only median TBT at batch size 32 falls in the range of roughly 150-300 ms, consistent with Figure 13a's PP curve for the paper's environment.

Poisson-process arrival-time generation is implemented so that each capacity/latency experiment consumes requests whose inter-arrival times are exponentially distributed with mean 1/QPS.

Code has been implemented that, given a target queries-per-second (QPS) rate, generates per-request arrival timestamps by drawing inter-arrival times from an Exponential(rate=QPS) distribution (equivalently, a Poisson arrival process), and attaches these timestamps to filtered dataset records.

The arrival-time generator supports a deterministic seed so that trace replay is reproducible across runs, and the empirical mean inter-arrival time over a generated trace matches 1/QPS within a small tolerance for the QPS sweep values used in §5.1 and §5.2.

Reproducible baselines: vLLM (prefill-prioritizing iteration-level batching with PagedAttention) and an Orca-like scheduler (iteration-level batching with hybrid batches) are integrated into the same harness for head-to-head comparison.

A shared scheduling harness abstracts request lifecycle, batch construction and metric collection so that alternative scheduler implementations (vLLM, Orca, Sarathi-Serve) can be swapped without changing model execution.
Code has been implemented that defines a common BaseScheduler interface (e.g. add_request, schedule, on_step_completed) that both the vLLM and Orca baseline schedulers subclass.

Code has been implemented so the harness routes an incoming request through arrival, prefill (possibly multi-iteration), decode (per-token iterations) and exit, and both baseline schedulers correctly transition requests through these states.

Code has been implemented that emits per-iteration and per-request telemetry (TTFT, TBT, batch composition, batch size, prefill/decode token counts) uniformly for both baseline schedulers, enabling head-to-head plots.

Code has been implemented that drives all schedulers from the same Poisson request generator over the openchat_sharegpt4 / arxiv_summarization traces, so a single benchmark script can invoke vLLM, Orca, and Sarathi-Serve with matching workloads.

The vLLM baseline implements Algorithm 2: iteration-level batching with prefill-prioritizing scheduling and PagedAttention-backed KV-cache management, forming either all-prefill or all-decode batches.

Code has been implemented that provides a VLLMScheduler class faithfully reproducing Algorithm 2: on each iteration it first tries to admit as many new requests as can_allocate_request permits and, if any were admitted, runs a prefill-only batch; otherwise it runs a decode-only batch over B.
Code has been implemented that enforces homogeneous batches in the vLLM baseline: a scheduled batch either contains only prefill work or only decode work; hybrid batches must not be produced.

Code has been implemented that integrates PagedAttention (blocked KV-cache with a block manager tracking free/allocated KV blocks per request) so that can_allocate_request returns True only when sufficient blocks are available for the incoming prompt.

Code has been implemented so vLLM admits new requests eagerly whenever KV blocks are available at the start of an iteration, immediately preempting the next decode step in favor of prefill computation.

A unit test verifies that with two decoding requests in flight and two new requests injected, the VLLMScheduler emits (i) a prefill-only batch containing the two new requests followed by (ii) a decode-only batch of size 4, matching Algorithm 2 lines 8–13.

Code has been implemented so that after each iteration the vLLM scheduler removes requests that emitted an end-of-sequence token (filter_finished_requests) and frees their KV blocks back to the paged block manager.

The vLLM baseline exposes a configurable max_batch_size that caps the number of concurrent requests in B, and the harness accepts values of at least 32, 64 and 128 as used by the throughput-latency sweep (Figure 12).
The Orca-like baseline implements iteration-level batching with hybrid prefill+decode batches, computing each new request's full prefill in a single iteration alongside ongoing decodes.

Code has been implemented that provides an OrcaScheduler class using FCFS iteration-level admission and constructing hybrid batches that combine ongoing decodes with the full prefill of any newly admitted request(s) in the same iteration.
Code has been implemented so an admitted prefill is executed in a single iteration in the Orca baseline — the scheduler never splits a prompt into chunks (distinguishing it from Sarathi-Serve).

Code has been implemented that admits new requests only when memory permits, using a max_num_tokens constraint of (max_sequence_length * batch_size) per iteration as described in §5.1 for the Orca baseline.

A unit test verifies that with two ongoing decodes A_d, B_d and two new requests C, D arriving, the OrcaScheduler emits a single hybrid batch {C_p, D_p, A_d, B_d} in the next iteration, matching the Orca timeline in Figure 7.

Code has been implemented so the model runner correctly handles hybrid batches for the Orca baseline: attention kernels dispatch prefill tokens against per-request KV caches while decode tokens attend to their own accumulated contexts within the same forward pass.
Both baselines are wired into the same head-to-head benchmarking pipeline and produce the qualitative behaviors reported in the paper's motivation section (Figure 1).

Code has been implemented so a single CLI flag (e.g. --scheduler {vllm,orca,sarathi}) switches the scheduling policy while keeping model, workload, hardware and seed fixed, enabling apples-to-apples comparisons.

Given identical seed, temperature and prompts, both the vLLM and Orca baselines produce identical output token sequences for a batch of at least four requests, confirming functional equivalence with only scheduling behavior differing.

Chunked-prefills splits a prefill into near-equal compute-sized chunks using paged FlashAttention-v2 kernels, correctly loads prior chunks' KV-cache for later chunks, and preserves prefill correctness relative to a non-chunked reference.

The chunk-splitting logic partitions a prefill prompt into a sequence of consecutive token spans whose sizes are governed by the scheduler's token budget and the number of ongoing decodes packed in the same iteration.

Code has been implemented for a `get_next_chunk_size(request, token_budget, current_batch_tokens)` (or equivalent) function on the chunked-prefill scheduler path that computes the number of remaining prefill tokens to schedule for a request in the current iteration.

`get_next_chunk_size` returns `min(token_budget - current_batch_tokens, prompt_tokens_remaining)` (clamped to zero) so the emitted chunk never exceeds the leftover token budget in the current hybrid batch.

For a prompt whose remaining prefill length is L and a token budget T with no decodes coscheduled, chunks emitted across successive iterations are near-equal in size: all but the last are exactly T tokens and the last is L mod T tokens.
Chunk boundaries advance monotonically per request across iterations (chunk N covers tokens [start_N, end_N) with start_{N+1} == end_N) so no prefill token is skipped or reprocessed.

The request state machine flips a request from `prefill` to `decode` only after the cumulative sum of scheduled chunk sizes equals the prompt length, so `is_prefill_complete(R)` becomes True on the iteration that emits the final chunk.
The paged FlashAttention-v2 backend is wired into Sarathi-Serve as the attention kernel used for chunked-prefill iterations and supports mixed prefill-chunk plus decode batches.

Code has been implemented for a paged chunked-prefill attention kernel invocation that dispatches to FlashAttention-v2 (e.g., `flash_attn_varlen_func` or an equivalent varlen entry point) with per-request start/end offsets for the query tokens in the current chunk.

The FlashAttention backend is selected by default for evaluation runs (matching the paper's statement that FlashAttention is used for all evaluations), and the FlashInfer backend is either present as an alternative code path or explicitly documented as optional.

The attention kernel accepts a `block_table` (paged KV-cache block index tensor) and a `context_lens` tensor per request so that a chunk of query length q attends to context length equal to (already-processed prefix + q).

The kernel applies a causal mask within the chunk's query tokens so that within a single chunk each query token attends only to itself and to earlier tokens in the same chunk plus all previously-committed KV-cache entries.

The kernel launch path handles hybrid batches in which one iteration contains a mix of chunk-prefill query tokens (q > 1 per request) and decode query tokens (q == 1 per request) with correct per-request query lengths.

A unit-level attention test drives the paged chunked-prefill kernel on a synthetic single-request prompt split into two chunks and verifies the returned per-token output tensor shape is `(q_chunk, num_heads, head_dim)` with no NaNs.
KV-cache produced during earlier chunks of a prefill is committed to the paged KV store and made visible to the attention kernel on later chunks of the same request.

Code has been implemented for a KV-cache write path that, after the linear QKV projection for a chunk, scatters the K and V tensors into the request's paged block table at offsets [chunk_start, chunk_end).

Per-request `context_lens` passed to the attention kernel on chunk N equals (sum of sizes of chunks 0..N-1) + (size of chunk N), so chunk N's queries attend over all previously-committed KV entries plus its own.

A test drives a two-chunk prefill of a 128-token prompt through the paged store and verifies that the K/V tensors materialized at positions [0, 64) after chunk 0 are byte-identical to the K/V tensors materialized at positions [0, 64) after chunk 1 (i.e., chunk-0 KV is not overwritten by chunk-1).
Paged block allocation for a chunked-prefill request grows the block table incrementally as each chunk is scheduled, without preallocating blocks for the entire prompt on the first chunk.

When a chunked-prefill request completes its final chunk and transitions to decode, subsequent decode iterations read from the same paged KV blocks written during the prefill chunks (no re-materialization required).
Chunked-prefill execution produces the same first-token output as an unchunked prefill of the same prompt, up to floating-point tolerance.

Code has been implemented for a numerical-equivalence test harness that runs a fixed prompt end-to-end through both (a) a full non-chunked prefill and (b) a chunked prefill with chunk size C, then compares per-position hidden states / logits at the final prompt token.

For chunk size 512 on a 2048-token prompt with Mistral-7B in fp16, the L-infinity norm between chunked and non-chunked final-position logits is below 5e-2 (numerical parity within fp16 attention tolerance).

For chunk size 512 and 1024, the argmax next-token predicted by chunked prefill matches the argmax next-token from non-chunked prefill on a suite of at least 8 held-out prompts of varying length from openchat_sharegpt4.

Greedy-decoded continuation of length 32 tokens is identical between chunked and non-chunked prefill for the same prompt (same random seed disabled, deterministic argmax), verifying that KV-cache written during chunked prefill matches what non-chunked prefill would have written.

The chunked-prefill code path accepts a configurable token budget / chunk size and does not hard-code a single chunk size, matching the paper's use of chunk sizes 512, 1024, 1536, and 2048 across experiments.
Code has been implemented so that the scheduler config exposes a `chunk_size` or `token_budget` parameter (integer, must be >= 1) that flows through to `get_next_chunk_size`.
The system runs end-to-end without kernel errors for chunk sizes {512, 1024, 1536, 2048} on a Mistral-7B prompt of length >= 4096, producing valid output tokens for each configuration.

When the caller requests a chunk_size not aligned to the FlashAttention tile size, the kernel still produces numerically correct output (attention correctness is not silently gated on chunk_size being a power-of-two).
Hybrid batches formed by combining a prefill chunk with concurrent decode queries are executed correctly by the chunked-prefill attention path.
